title: Majorana Edge-to-bound State Transition in Interferometric Superconductor Rings
authors: Xiangyu Bi, Aoshen Yang, Hongzi Cao, Ganyu Chen, Yuqiang Fang, Zeya Li, Qizheng Sun, Junwei Huang, Da Wang, Fuqiang Huang, Toshiya Ideue, Qianghua Wang, Yoshihiro Iwasa, Hongtao Yuan
abstract: Manipulating flux quanta in topological superconductors is central to vortex braiding in quantum computing. Their interferometric superconducting rings can host either topologically protected edge states with fluxes confined inside the central hollow area or vortex bound states in flux cores at the annulus walls. Here we demonstrate a strategy to drive topological edge states into vortex bound states by tuning the relative scale of vortex size and annulus width in nano-ring interferometric device on 2M-WS$_2$ topological superconductor. Near its superconducting transition where the coherence length exceeds the annulus width, Little-Parks oscillations exhibit expected periods for flux bundles in ring-center, consistent with edge states residing at inner and outer rims of the annulus. Upon cooling, where the coherence length shrinks below the annulus width, the unexpectedly increased oscillation period reflects multiple fluxes distributed along annulus region in flux necklace configuration, implying a transition from extended edge states to localized vortex bound states. Ginzburg-Landau simulations and local density-of-states calculations with Bogoliubov-de Gennes equations reveal that large values for both Ginzburg-Landau parameter and flux-pinning energy are vital for such a transition. Our findings provide a novel strategy for understanding flux manipulation towards flux braiding and topological quantum computing.
summary: This work reports on a novel method to switch between two distinct magnetic flux configurations—a flux bundle and a flux necklace—in superconducting nano-rings made of 2M-WS2. The transition is controlled by tuning the temperature, which alters the superconducting coherence length relative to the ring geometry. This transition is theoretically linked to the emergence of Majorana zero modes, offering a promising platform for topological quantum computation.
main_problem: The paper demonstrates a controllable transition between topologically protected edge states (flux bundle) and localized vortex bound states (flux necklace) in superconducting rings.
main_result: By tuning temperature to change the coherence length relative to the annulus width, the system can be driven from a flux bundle state to a flux necklace state, which is associated with Majorana zero modes.
method: The study combines transport measurements (Little-Parks oscillations) with advanced theoretical simulations, including Ginzburg-Landau and Bogoliubov-de Gennes equations.
model_or_system: The physical system is an interferometric nano-ring device made from the topological superconductor 2M-WS2. The model analyzes the competition between flux quantization in the ring center versus localization along the annulus walls.
key_observables: Little-Parks oscillation period, local density of states (LDOS) zero-energy peaks, and the ratio of coherence length to annulus width ($\xi_{ab}/w$).
important_parameters: Temperature (controlling $\xi_{ab}$), annulus width ($w$), and the superconducting transition temperature ($T_c$).
main_assumptions: The transition is governed by the relative scales of the coherence length and annulus width, and the localized states are assumed to host Majorana zero modes.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the comparison between flux bundle and flux necklace magnetic flux distributions, the temperature dependence of magnetoresistance oscillations, and the resulting zero-energy peaks in the LDOS.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical system and the two competing flux states, uses Little-Parks oscillations to experimentally identify the transition regime, and then employs TDGL and BdG simulations to theoretically confirm the mechanism and the emergence of Majorana bound states.
why_interesting: The controlled switching between different topological flux configurations provides a concrete, tunable platform for realizing and studying Majorana zero modes, which are central to topological quantum computing.
